cues.en: Great. All right. So I'm happy to be here today to talk about why performance really matters. So before I do, I want to talk about our favorite family, The Simpsons. And so hopefully most of you are familiar with this family. This show has been on the air for an incredible amount of time. But things have changed in this incredible amount of time. So this is The Simpsons today, but The Simpsons actually premiered in the 80s. And in the 80s, they looked really different.
cues.zh: 太好了。好的。今天我很高兴能在这里谈谈为什么性能真的很重要。在开始之前，我想聊聊我们最爱的家庭——《辛普森一家》。希望大多数人都熟悉这个家庭。这部剧播出时间长得惊人。但在这么长的时间里，事情发生了变化。这是今天的《辛普森一家》，但《辛普森一家》其实首播于80年代。而在80年代，他们看起来完全不同。

cues.en: I would say they've improved substantially over the years. And this sort of evolution turns out to have been echoed not only in Simpsons, but also in our computers. So if you have a smartphone today, that smartphone today, it may have six cores, each running over two gigahertz, 64-bit processor, four gigs or more of RAM. You compare this to the world in the 80s.
cues.zh: 我得说这些年来他们进步了不少。而这种演变不仅体现在《辛普森一家》上，也映照在我们的电脑上。所以如果你今天有一部智能手机，那部手机可能有六个核心，每个运行超过2GHz，64位处理器，4GB或更多内存。把这个和80年代的世界对比一下。

cues.en: We had computers that were vastly less advanced, where the speed is measured in megahertz, the processors were 16-bit at best, sometimes even 8-bit, and the amount of RAM was much smaller. In fact, if you divide these out, if you put one on top of the other, you can see, roughly speaking, that today's computers are about 3,000 times larger, faster, better than computers in the past. So before the 80s, when computers were so slow,
cues.zh: 我们当时的计算机远没有这么先进，速度以兆赫计量，处理器最多 16 位，有时甚至只有 8 位，内存也小得多。事实上，如果算一下比例，把两者放在一起比较，大致可以说，今天的计算机比过去的计算机大约大 3000 倍、快 3000 倍、好 3000 倍。所以在 80 年代以前，计算机还那么慢的时候，

cues.en: basically programmers had to resort to languages that were designed to have as little overhead as possible and to be as close to the metal as imaginable. So these robots are meant to represent these various programming languages, starting with assembler, moving into Fortran and C and C++, and I like to call these the metal languages. These languages by design have virtually no overhead, and that was really important because computers were just so slow. However, in the intervening years,
cues.zh: 基本上，程序员只能借助那些被设计成开销尽可能小、尽可能贴近硬件的语言。所以这些机器人代表的就是各种编程语言，从汇编开始，到 Fortran、C 和 C++，我喜欢把它们叫作金属语言。这些语言在设计上几乎没有额外开销，而这一点非常重要，因为当时的计算机实在太慢了。然而，在此后的这些年里，

cues.en: We've been on this performance ride. So right starting around the late 70s and early 80s, computers started getting faster and faster. And so what happened was we had these twin trends that were occurring. One, the number of transistors was going up at a rate of roughly twice every 18 months, known as Moore's law. I draw your attention to the fact that this is a long scale. So it looks like it's linear, but it's really, really super linear. It's going up by exponentially.
cues.zh: 我们一直处在性能飙升的进程中。从 70 年代末、80 年代初开始，计算机开始越来越快。于是出现了两个并行的趋势。其一，晶体管数量大约每 18 个月翻一番，这就是摩尔定律。请注意，这是对数尺度。所以它看起来像线性的，但实际上是超级线性的，是在指数级增长。

cues.en: And at the same time, clock speeds were going up. And so what happened was these chips were getting more and more gates on them, more and more transistors, and they were getting faster and faster. And so the effect was every year, you could literally go and buy a new computer and your computer would just run faster. So what the implication was, was that these metal languages maybe were no longer necessary because computers were getting faster and faster and we could afford to be
cues.zh: 与此同时，时钟频率也在不断提升。于是情况就是，这些芯片上的门电路越来越多，晶体管越来越多，速度也越来越快。结果就是，每年你都可以直接去买一台新电脑，而你的电脑就是会跑得更快。所以这意味着，这些元语言也许不再必要了，因为计算机越来越快，我们大可承受在构建这些语言时

cues.en: a little more slack with how we built these languages. In the 80s and the 90s, there was this period of time where a bunch of other languages came out that were vastly less efficient than C or C++, starting with Perl and including languages like Tickle, TK, PHP, Ruby, and Python. I like to call these the irrational exuberance languages. These were languages where people simply thought things were just going to get faster and faster forever.
cues.zh: 稍微宽松一些。在80年代和90年代，有那么一段时期，涌现了一大批效率远低于C或C++的语言，从Perl开始，还包括Tcl、TK、PHP、Ruby和Python。我喜欢把这类语言称为“非理性繁荣语言”。在这些语言里，人们简单地以为事情会永远越来越快。

cues.en: And so it was OK to have pretty substantial inefficiencies. So I'm going to focus today on Python when I'm talking about these, but all of these languages share very similar features. So the arrow is pointing to Homer's stomach, and that's because all of these languages are kind of loaded in terms of the amount of space they consume. So you might think that an int, for example, is a relatively small amount of information. It's a small number of bytes. And in C++, the size of an int
cues.zh: 所以存在相当严重的低效也问题不大。今天我讲这些的时候会聚焦Python，但这些语言都有非常相似的特征。箭头指向荷马的肚子，这是因为这些语言在占用空间上都相当“有分量”。你可能会觉得，比如一个int，信息量相对较小，就几个字节。在C++里，一个int的大小

cues.en: is going to be four. However, in Python, that same int is actually 24 bytes. So it's six times larger than it needs to be. This is true for really, it's just true across the board. So it's not just numbers. So an empty list in C++ would be 24 bytes. And in Python, it turns out it's 56. So more than double. And then my favorite example is an empty dict. That is to say an associative array or a map. The size of it in C++ is 24 bytes.
cues.zh: 是四。然而在Python里，同一个int实际上是24字节。也就是说，它是所需大小的六倍。这普遍成立，真的，这是全面的事实。不只是数字。C++里一个空列表是24字节。而在Python里，结果是56字节。翻了一倍还多。然后我最喜欢的例子是空dict，也就是关联数组或映射。它在C++里的大小是24字节。

cues.en: In Python, today, it's 64, so it's nearly three times as much, but this is the result of Python putting on a little bit of a diet up until just a year or two ago. It was 240 bytes, so it's 10 times more memory. I know this is suspiciously close to Homer Simpson's own weight. Definitely, Python and these other languages are inefficient in terms of memory consumption, but they're also
cues.zh: 在今天的 Python 中，是 64，所以差不多是三倍，但这是 Python 直到一两年前稍微“瘦身”后的结果。以前是 240 字节，也就是 10 倍的内存。我知道这跟荷马·辛普森自己的体重近得有点可疑。确实，Python 和其他这些语言在内存消耗上很低效，但它们也同样

cues.en: famously inefficient in terms of performance. So they're infamous that they're slow. And so just to give you a sense of how slow they can be, here is a sample bit of code that does matrix matrix multiply. So this is the naive matrix matrix multiply just expressed in a loop in Python. And I want to thank Charles Leiserson for this example.
cues.zh: 在性能上出了名地低效。所以它们臭名昭著地慢。为了让你感受一下它们能有多慢，这里有一段做矩阵乘法的示例代码。这就是用 Python 循环直接表达的朴素矩阵乘法。我要感谢 Charles Leiserson 提供这个例子。

cues.en: Here is a graph showing the difference in applying different techniques to this Python code. I'm sorry, to matrix multiply. If Python is one, C, just writing it in C is 47 times faster. When you apply all the optimizations that you can do in C and that are included in standard C libraries, it's over 60,000 times faster. This is a pretty big gap. Maybe it seemed to make sense when Python
cues.zh: 这张图展示了在这段 Python 代码上应用不同技术的差异。抱歉，是矩阵乘法。如果 Python 是 1，C，光是用 C 写就快 47 倍。当你用上 C 里能做、且标准 C 库自带的所有优化时，它快了超过 60,000 倍。这是个相当大的差距。也许当年看起来还说得通，那时 Python

cues.en: was going to get faster by virtue of the fact that we were on this ride, and this ride seemed like it was going on forever. But unfortunately, the ride did not go on forever, and in fact has stopped. So we were here, but now we're here. The ride is over. So starting around 2010, the ride just ended. And what happened was this trend that we...
cues.zh: 会因为我们搭上了这趟快车而变快，而这趟快车看起来会一直开下去。但不幸的是，这趟车并没有一直开下去，事实上它停了。所以我们曾在这里，但现在我们在这里。这趟车结束了。所以大约从 2010 年开始，这趟车就戛然而止了。发生的情况是，我们……的这个趋势

cues.en: hoped and expected was going to continue drawing this line out. You can see the dotted lines for transistors and clock speed. What happened was we still got more transistors. The number of transistors continued. That is to say, this is Moore's law, and Moore's law has not yet ended. It has to end eventually, but it has not yet ended. However, what did end was scaling of clock speed. And this is referred to as Dennard scaling. And Dennard scaling has simply run out of steam.
cues.zh: 人们曾希望并期待这条线会继续延伸下去。你能看到晶体管和时钟频率对应的虚线。实际情况是，我们仍然获得了更多晶体管。晶体管数量继续增长。也就是说，这就是摩尔定律，而摩尔定律还没有结束。它最终一定会结束，但现在还没有。然而，真正结束的是时钟频率的缩放。这被称为 Dennard scaling。而 Dennard scaling 已经彻底难以为继。

cues.en: for a variety of reasons, and I'm not going to go into those here, but in short, the chips are basically too hot or they leak too much voltage, so it's not really possible to clock these things up in any realistic way. Things were great in the 80s. If you needed to speed up your program, you just didn't do anything, you could literally just go and have a beach vacation and wait, and your code would run faster by virtue of the fact that time had elapsed and computers had gotten faster. But today, you have to work.
cues.zh: 原因有很多，我在这里不展开，但简而言之，芯片基本上要么太热，要么漏电压太多，所以现实中基本不可能把这些东西的时钟频率提上去。80 年代很美好。如果你需要让程序变快，你什么都不用做，真的可以直接去海滩度假等着；随着时间过去、计算机变快，你的代码自然就跑得更快了。但今天，你得干活了。

cues.en: Today, it's really hard. And so the only opportunity Homer has for a duff is going to be in the form of an energy drink at this point. So I'm going to explain right now why performance has gotten so complicated and why we're going to have to do new things to get us out of this, these problems that we've in some way created for ourselves. So here is the way a typical performance evaluation goes, where somebody says, I have an idea, like Homer has an idea, I'm going to speed up a program.
cues.zh: 今天，这真的很难。所以现在，Homer 唯一能来一口 Duff 的机会，就是能量饮料了。所以我现在要解释，为什么性能变得这么复杂，以及为什么我们必须做新事情，才能摆脱这些问题——这些在某种程度上是我们自己给自己制造的问题。典型的性能评估过程是这样的：有人说，我有个想法——就像 Homer 有个想法一样——我要加速一个程序。

cues.en: So Homer goes and rewrites some code, changes around some things, maybe refactors some stuff out, and eventually ends up with an optimized version. At least he hopes it's going to be optimized. So he goes and he runs the programs. There's A, the original program at A prime, the optimized version. A takes 90 seconds. Great. A prime takes 87.5 seconds. So Homer says, woo, 2.8% faster. All right. So his genius idea to optimize the code was successful.
cues.zh: Homer 去重写了一些代码，改动了周围的一些东西，也许还重构掉了一些东西，最终得到了一个优化版本。至少他希望它是优化过的。于是他去运行程序。有 A，原始程序，和 A prime，优化版本。A 耗时 90 秒。很好。A prime 耗时 87.5 秒。于是 Homer 说，哇，快了 2.8%。好。他那个优化代码的天才想法成功了。

cues.en: or so it seems. So it is faster. The question is why, why is it faster? So of course, just a total accident. So what could have happened was this interaction between the changes that Homer made and the underlying hardware. So there's a lovely paper that a few of my colleagues wrote back in 2009. The paper has a wonderful title, Producing Wrong Data Without Doing Anything Obviously Wrong.
cues.zh: 或者说看起来是这样。它确实更快了。问题是为什么，为什么更快？当然，纯属意外。实际可能发生的是 Homer 所做的改动与底层硬件之间的相互作用。我几位同事在 2009 年写过一篇很棒的论文。论文有个绝妙的标题：《在不做任何明显错误的事情的情况下产生错误数据》。

cues.en: And it gathered together a bunch of information showing that very modest changes, things that you would never expect would have a big impact can actually have a gigantic impact on performance. And so things like changing the link order, that is to say, if you have a makefile and you have a bunch of .Os, if you move those .Os around, that changes where the functions end up in memory. Likewise, if you change the environment variables,
cues.zh: 它汇集了一堆信息，表明非常微小的改动——那些你绝不会想到会有大影响的事情——实际上可能对性能产生巨大影响。比如改变链接顺序，也就是说，如果你有一个 makefile 和一堆 .o 文件，如果你把这些 .o 文件挪来挪去，就会改变函数在内存中的最终位置。同样，如果你改变环境变量，

cues.en: the environment variables actually are loaded into memory when you load your program and then the stack starts after it, so it moves the program stack, which means the data has moved around. So you might think, well, okay, those are fine. They seem like they shouldn't have any effect, but it turns out they can have a gigantic effect. They can have an effect that is larger than the impact of no optimization to full optimization, which is you can get plus or minus 40% swings. So let me explain what's going on.
cues.zh: 环境变量实际上会在加载程序时被载入内存，然后栈从其后开始，所以它会移动程序栈，也就意味着数据被挪动了位置。所以你可能会想，好吧，这些都没问题。它们看起来不该有任何影响，但事实证明它们能产生巨大的影响。它们的影响可能比从不优化到完全优化的影响还大，也就是说，你可能会看到正负 40% 的波动。那么让我解释一下这是怎么回事。

cues.en: Here's an example. So suppose in the original program A, before Homer made his changes, there's two hot lines of code, and they both match map to the same cache set. So modern hardware, because especially because things have run out of steam, they've gotten quite complex in an effort to extract every bit of performance out. And so there are these on chip caches, the caches are organized into sets, and they're not like they don't necessarily take
cues.zh: 这里有个例子。假设在原始程序A中，在Homer做出修改之前，有两行热点代码，它们都映射到同一个缓存集。现代硬件，尤其是因为单核性能已经遇到瓶颈，为了榨取每一点性能，变得相当复杂。所以有了这些片上缓存，缓存被组织成组，它们并不一定采用

cues.en: full advantage of the whole size of the cache. And if you have a bunch of things that map to the set, it can overflow it and you get a result called a conflict, which means that the cache is no longer efficient and you have to go fetch information from memory, which is slow. However, when Homer made his changes and made his optimized version, it could have been the case that just by sheer accident, he ended up making it so that things that used to map to the same set no longer do.
cues.zh: 充分利用缓存的全部容量。如果有一堆东西映射到同一个集合，就可能把它撑爆，产生所谓的冲突，也就是说缓存不再高效，你得回到内存里去取信息，而那很慢。不过，当 Homer 做了改动、做出优化版本时，也可能只是纯属巧合，他恰好让原本映射到同一集合的东西不再这样了。

cues.en: and there's something that's either cold or there's just nothing there at all, resulting in no conflict. Going from a conflict to no conflict could mean that your program is faster simply because of the cache. You might think, well, this is maybe the only issue to deal with, but it turns out the cache is not the only thing to blame. There are lots of performance-sensitive micro-architectural features on modern chips that are influenced by program addresses or data addresses.
cues.zh: 有些东西要么是冷的，要么压根就不存在，因此不会产生冲突。从有冲突变成无冲突，可能仅仅因为缓存，你的程序就变快了。你可能会想，这也许就是唯一要处理的问题了，但事实证明，缓存并不是唯一的罪魁祸首。现代芯片上有许多对性能敏感的微架构特性，都会受到程序地址或数据地址的影响。

cues.en: These include a branch predictor, which tries to predict which way a branch is going to go. Is it the if condition or the else condition? That's based on tables that are indexed by program counter location. There's a thing called the TLB, which maps your virtual addresses to physical addresses. If you have
cues.zh: 其中包括分支预测器，它试图预测分支会走哪条路。是走 if 条件还是 else 条件？这基于以程序计数器位置为索引的表。还有一个叫 TLB 的东西，它把虚拟地址映射到物理地址。如果你有

cues.en: something that used to fit in the TLB, which is a kind of cache. And now because you've moved things around, things straddle pages and they no longer fit in TLB, that can seriously degrade performance, or vice versa. You could make things accidentally fit and then things get better. There's a thing called a branch target predictor. There's a prefecture. Suffice it to say that there's lots of stuff going on and it's quite complicated, right? In addition, optimizations themselves over time have kind of run out of steam.
cues.zh: 某个原本能放进 TLB（它也是一种缓存）的东西。现在因为你把东西挪来挪去，数据跨了页，不再能放进 TLB，这可能会严重拖慢性能，反过来也一样。你也可能碰巧让它们放得下，然后性能就变好了。还有一个叫分支目标预测器的东西。还有预取器。这么说吧，里面发生的事情很多，而且相当复杂，对吧？此外，优化本身随着时间推移，也渐渐后劲不足了。

cues.en: So if you factor out all of these layout changes, it turns out that across a vast array of these applications that people use to test compilers, the speedups that you get that are statistically significant are really quite small. So you really can't count on much assistance from the compiler to really get you out of this problem. So performance is really brittle. If you change something,
cues.zh: 所以，如果把所有这些布局变化都排除掉，结果发现，在人们用来测试编译器的大量应用中，你能获得的、具有统计显著性的加速其实非常小。所以你真的不能指望编译器帮多大忙，来让你摆脱这个问题。所以性能真的很脆弱。如果你改动一点东西，

cues.en: You can get dramatic swings in performance, and the performance swings you get are really vastly larger than the compiler can even produce. So Homer needs help. Homer can't rely on compiler optimizations anymore, can't rely on computers getting faster every year, and unfortunately, tools have not kept up. So let me show you an example of where tools fail for Homer. So suppose Homer
cues.zh: 性能就可能出现剧烈波动，而这些波动幅度远远大于编译器所能带来的变化。所以 Homer 需要帮助。Homer 不能再依赖编译器优化，也不能再依赖计算机每年变快，而不幸的是，工具并没有跟上。下面我举个例子，看看工具在哪些地方帮不了 Homer。假设 Homer

cues.en: is in modern day 2020, it has an idea for an app. And Homer's idea for the app is this great idea because it involves cats and the internet. So the idea is you go on your smartphone and you take a picture of a cat and then it gets sent to some servers and it comes back and it returns all the images that match this cat in the form of memes. So this is great. Clearly it's going to take over the internet. He has a great idea for the name. He's going to call it ogle.

You take a picture, it sends it to the ogle servers, and in Homer's genius move, it saves the image in the database so it can be retrieved later by other ogle users. It then goes and finds similar images and sends the results back.

So in a sense, when you go to Ogle, it's going to create two separate threads, one of which is going to go and do some compression of the image, maybe shrink it down in size to the thumbnail or something. Of course, this is the whole process and they sync at the end. I've simplified things a lot, not just in the form of putting these in icons, but also, we're talking about concurrency. Concurrency involves these things like locks to prevent things from happening simultaneously and clapping each other. Real applications, obviously, are more complex. Fine.
cues.zh: 另一个线程实际上可以提取特征，用这些特征查找其他图片，然后执行搜索，再把结果发回给用户。当然，整个过程最终会进行同步。我已经把事情大幅简化了，不只是把这些步骤画成图标这么简单，我们讨论的还涉及并发。并发会涉及锁之类的机制，防止多个操作同时发生并互相冲突。实际应用显然要复杂得多。就这样。

So a software profiler essentially goes and takes your program and produces statistics about it, and those are meant to inform you as to what you should do to make the program run faster.
cues.zh: 假设Homer去开发了这个应用，发布出去，大家都喜欢Ogle，但后来Ogle变得特别慢。这真的很糟心。Homer很难过。Homer该怎么办呢？Homer通常会做的，也是我们原则上都应该做的，就是去用软件性能分析器。软件性能分析器 basically 会拿你的程序跑一遍，生成统计数据，这些数据旨在告诉你该怎么做才能让程序跑得更快。

cues.en: So the big ideas in software profilers really came out in the eighties and nineties. Um, and this is a bit of a caricature, but to a first approximation, this is what profilers do. They do something like report the number of calls that you make to each function. Um, and they report the runtime for each function. So you get these statistics and what you're supposed to do with them nominally is you find the code that is frequently executed and it runs for a long time.
cues.zh: 软件性能分析器里的核心思想其实是在八九十年代提出来的。嗯，这有点夸张，但粗略来说，分析器就是这么干的。它们会做一些类似报告每个函数被调用了多少次的事情。嗯，还会报告每个函数的运行时间。你拿到这些统计数据，名义上你应该做的就是找到那些频繁执行、运行时间又长的代码。

cues.en: And that's the code where you should spend your time, right? That's what you optimize. And that's going to make your program run faster. So the question is, when we do this in Augal, is this actually going to help? Would this speed up Augal? So suppose Homer takes the profiler, gets the information, finds the code that lasts the longest, that runs the most time, and he applies it to Augal. And after a lot of effort, it turns out, oh, no.
cues.zh: 那才是你该花时间的地方，对吧？那就是你要优化的东西。这样就能让你的程序跑得更快。所以问题是，我们在Augal里这么做，真的会有帮助吗？这能让Augal提速吗？假设Homer拿着分析器，拿到信息，找到运行时间最长、耗时最多的代码，然后把它应用到Augal上。费了好大一番功夫之后，结果发现，哦不。

cues.en: What he did was he optimized the loading blinky part. And so that's not really helping ogle go any faster. But what he did was he found frequently executed code. That loading thing is quite frequently executed. And it runs for a long time. In fact, it runs for the longest time. It runs from the beginning to the end of the whole ogle process. So optimizing that is clearly a mistake. That's not what he should have been optimizing.
cues.zh: 他其实是去优化了加载时一闪一闪的动画，但这并没有真正让 ogle 变快一点。但他确实找到了频繁执行的代码，那个加载程序执行得非常频繁，而且运行时间很长。事实上，它的运行时间是最长的，贯穿了整个 ogle 进程的始末。所以去优化它显然是个错误，那根本不是他应该优化的东西。

cues.en: Right? And it turns out that existing profilers just don't do a great job of finding the important code in modern applications. In modern applications, we care about things like latency. We have programs that run forever, conceptually. They're parallel, they're asynchronous, they're concurrent, and the existing profilers just have not kept up. They're essentially still stuck back in the 80s. So we need to do better. So the question is, what would speed up ogle? Right? So we would like to know, ideally,
cues.zh: 对吧？事实证明，现有的性能分析器在现代应用中根本无法很好地找出关键代码。在现代应用中，我们关注的是延迟这类的指标。从概念上讲，我们的程序是永不停止运行的，它们是并行的、异步的、并发的，而现有的性能分析器根本没有跟上步伐，它们本质上还停留在 80 年代。所以我们必须做得更好。那么问题来了，怎样才能让 ogle 提速？对吧？所以理想情况下，我们想知道的是：

cues.en: imagine there was some magic pixie dust that we could sprinkle over the yawgle source code, and it would land on the code where Homer needed to spend his optimization efforts. Suppose it was this magnifying glass, that is to say the search part, that would be great. I would tell Homer, go work on this, it's guaranteed to produce a certain result. What would this information look like? Maybe not going to look like sparkles on your source code, that might not be as helpful as you'd want.
cues.zh: 想象一下，如果有一种神奇的小仙子魔法粉，我们把它撒在 yawgle 的源代码上，它就会落在 Homer 真正需要花精力去优化的代码上。假设它落在这个放大镜上，也就是搜索那部分，那就太棒了。我就可以告诉 Homer：去搞这块，保证能出效果。那这类信息到底会以什么形式呈现？肯定不会是真在你的源码上闪闪发光，真那样可能也没你想象的那么有用。

cues.en: So what we propose is something we call a causal profile. So causal profile tells you where your optimizations will make a difference and tells you how much of a difference they'll make. So suppose you've got these components of your program and you've got a graph on the X axis, you've got the speed up, that is the speed up for an individual component. And on the Y axis, you've got the program speed up or the improvement in throughput or the reduction in latency. And we'll talk more about that in a minute.
cues.zh: 所以我们提出的是所谓的因果剖面。因果剖面能告诉你哪些优化会起作用，以及它们能带来多大改善。假设你有程序的这些组件，X轴上是加速比，也就是单个组件的加速比。Y轴上是程序加速比，或者吞吐量的提升，或者延迟的降低。我们稍后会详细讨论。

cues.en: The kind of graph that you'd like to see is, look, if I spend a lot of time on the search part, I'm going to get a bang for my buck that's pretty high up until a certain point when it plateaus. So I'll know to optimize and I'll know when it's time to stop my optimization efforts. Similarly, I'll find code where I shouldn't spend any time. It turns out this compression thing maybe is never going to be a bottleneck no matter how fast I make it. So this is really useful to know. I'm not going to work on that at all.
cues.zh: 你希望看到的图表是这样的：如果我在搜索部分花大量时间，收益会很高，直到某个点后趋于平稳。这样我就知道该优化，也知道何时停止优化。同样，我会找到不该花时间的代码。结果发现，这个压缩部分无论我把它做得多快，可能永远不会成为瓶颈。所以知道这点很有用。我完全不会去动它。

cues.en: And I might find other code, like the indexing part, feature extraction, where, yes, I don't get as big a bang for my buck as with the search. But if I keep working on it, I'll make the program run faster and faster. So this is great. It tells you, really, if I speed up a particular component by a certain amount, I will get a certain speed up. And so I can plan my effort accordingly. So this is all terrific. It would be wonderful to have.
cues.zh: 我还可能发现其他代码，比如索引部分、特征提取，虽然收益不如搜索部分大，但只要我继续优化，程序就会跑得越来越快。这很棒。它告诉你，如果我把某个组件加速一定量，就能获得一定的程序加速。这样我就能相应地规划精力。这一切都很棒，能有这样的工具就好了。

cues.en: The challenge is how do we get this information? So what I want to know is how I do a certain change, right? I get this effect. So I'm going to describe something that's impossible first and then show you how to make it possible. So the impossible part is we're going to run experiments and we call these performance experiments. So these experiments depend on magic. So if we could magically speed up every component, we could speed it up and then observe
cues.zh: 挑战在于我们如何获取这些信息？我想知道的是，我如何进行某项改动？然后得到这个效果。所以我打算先描述一件不可能的事，再展示如何让它变得可能。不可能的部分是，我们要做实验，称之为性能实验。这些实验依赖于魔法。如果我们能神奇地加速每个组件，就能加速它然后观察

cues.en: what the effect is, right? So we speed it up by a little bit and we get a certain speed up. We speed it up a little more, we observe another speed up, right? And so on, right? And then we just do this for every component. We see, well, if I sped that up, that has no effect and so on, right? And then we can use this to build our graph. Unfortunately, we're gonna have to do this without magic because magic is not a thing. Also, if we have magic, this is what we would do. We would magically optimize the things to zero.
cues.zh: 效果是什么，对吧？我们稍微加速一点，得到一定的加速效果。再加速一点，观察到另一个加速效果，对吧？以此类推。然后我们对每个组件都这样做。我们发现，如果我加速那个，那没有效果，等等。然后我们可以用这个来构建我们的图。不幸的是，我们得在没有魔法的情况下做这件事，因为魔法不存在。另外，如果我们有魔法，我们会这样做。我们会神奇地把东西优化到零。

cues.en: and it would be awesome. But magic doesn't exist, sorry Homer. So we need another way. So how can we do these performance experiments without magic? So the key insight that causal profiling depends on is using something that we call virtual speed ups. So a virtual speed up is kind of like a theory of relativity thing. What we're gonna do is we're gonna give the effect of speeding something up by slowing everything else down that's running concurrently with it. So here,
cues.zh: 那会很棒。但魔法不存在，抱歉 Homer。所以我们需要另一种方法。那么，如何在没有魔法的情况下做这些性能实验？因果分析依赖的关键洞察是使用我们称之为虚拟加速的东西。虚拟加速有点像相对论的概念。我们要做的是，通过减慢与某物并发运行的其他所有东西，来达到加速它的效果。所以在这里，

cues.en: when we go and we speed up virtually the transmission, what we're really doing is we're slowing other things down. It turns out it's really easy to slow things down, just harder to speed them up. So when we slow those things down, we can then observe the resulting slowdown, and that slowdown corresponds to the speed up, the results we would have gotten had we actually sped that thing up. So we get a point in our causal graph.
cues.zh: 当我们虚拟地加速传输时，我们实际上是在减慢其他东西。事实证明，减慢东西很容易，加速则更难。所以当我们减慢那些东西时，我们就能观察到由此产生的减速，而这个减速对应于加速——即如果我们真的加速了那个东西会得到的结果。这样我们就得到了因果图上的一个点。

cues.en: And we can just rinse and repeat. We do this over and over again. We observe the results and we build out the graph. And we'll do this for component by component, just as described before. So here we observe the effects and eventually we get all the results for the red one. And finally, we do the same for everything. All right, so there's our causal profile. So this is great. Now I've spoken about this in terms of program speed up, but
cues.zh: 我们可以不断重复这个过程。反复执行，观察结果并构建出关系图。然后像之前说的那样，逐个组件进行。这里我们观察效果，最终得到红色部分的全部结果。最后，对所有部分都做同样的事。好了，这就是我们的因果画像。很棒。现在我说的是程序提速，但

And the ogle server conceptually runs forever and making the ogle server terminate quickly is not a goal, right? That's not what we want. So what we actually care about is we care about things like how long does it take between sending a request to ogle and getting a response back. And this is referred to as latency, right? So the other thing we might care about is
cues.zh: 对于一个本就不打算结束的程序来说，这不一定说得通。ogle服务器概念上是永远运行的，让ogle服务器快速终止并不是目标，对吧？那不是我们想要的。所以我们真正关心的是，比如从向ogle发送请求到收到响应需要多长时间。这被称为延迟，对吧？另一件我们可能关心的是

So when you're doing causal profiling, you don't just run causal profiling with an ordinary program without any changes. You have to make some slight annotations to the program. We call these annotations progress point. So progress point. So for example, suppose Homer wants the throughput to be higher for sending responses back. So to optimize this,
cues.zh: 结果返回得有多快？这些东西被服务的速度有多快？这叫做吞吐量。所以做因果分析时，你不能对一个普通程序不做任何修改就直接跑。你必须对程序做一些轻微的标注。我们把这些标注称为进度点。进度点。举个例子，假设Homer希望发送响应的吞吐量更高。那么为了优化这一点，

cues.en: hover has to market as a progress point. And in our implementation, this is just a macro. cues.zh: 从某种形式，比如Python数组转换成NumPy数组，后者要小得多也密集得多。这是金属表示法。但结果发现这本来就是一个NumPy数组。NumPy的均匀随机数生成器已经创建了NumPy数组。所以它实际上是在分配一个数组来复制进去，复制旧数组，然后释放那个数组。这就是锯齿状的凸起。那个峰值就是它分配的时候

cues.zh: 除了原本所需的空间外，还要再分配一块新空间来存放副本，然后它把这个空间释放掉了。这个问题同样很容易修复。我们要做的就是去掉 np.array 调用。现在，不再写成对这个东西调用 np.array，而是直接把它删掉。这实际上在语义上完全等价。可以看到，这带来了很大影响。突然之间，CPU 占用率大幅下降。内存使用仍然很高。

cues.en: It's 85%, but it is over a smaller denominator, and that sawtooth pattern has gone away. You can see that it went from one gigabyte to 860 megabytes in total memory usage, and the runtime also dropped from 6.3 seconds to 5.4 seconds.

cues.en: It's quite easy to understand and it's nice and clean. Most of the scripting languages, in fact, all of them now have this phenomenon that's called deferred signal delivery. Like some previous profilers, Scalene is a sampling-based profiler, which means it periodically interrupts the Python program and checks where it is at that moment, and it does this over and over and over again.
cues.zh: 这很容易理解，而且简洁明了。大多数脚本语言，实际上现在所有这类语言都有一种现象叫做延迟信号传递。像之前的许多分析器一样，Scalene是一个基于采样的分析器，这意味着它会定期中断Python程序，检查它当时执行到哪里，如此反复不断。

cues.en: This allows it to operate with low overhead while getting pretty precise information. This is fine if you have code that's running exclusively in Python. If you send a signal every 0.1 seconds, for example, it will get delivered roughly every 0.1 seconds, as you would hope. However, Python itself actually doesn't just deliver the signals that come from your timer, it delays them until Python regains control.
cues.zh: 这使得它能在低开销下运行，同时获取相当精确的信息。如果你的代码完全在Python中运行，这没问题。比如，如果你每0.1秒发送一个信号，它大约会每0.1秒被传递一次，正如你所期望的。然而，Python本身实际上并不只是传递来自定时器的信号，它会延迟这些信号，直到Python重新获得控制权。

cues.en: So if you execute some code that actually runs in C++ or C like NumPy, none of those signals get delivered until that code finishes executing. So this is unfortunate because from the perspective of a profiler, nothing has happened. Basically, there'll be no information gathered, and it could be the bulk of the time that your program is actually executing, and it'll get no information. And worse, it'll mislead you. So you could have a program
cues.zh: 所以如果你执行一些实际上运行在 C++ 或类似 NumPy 的 C 代码里的代码，那么在这段代码执行完之前，那些信号都不会被送达。这很不幸，因为从分析器的角度看，什么都没发生。基本上收集不到任何信息，而这可能占了你程序实际执行的大部分时间，却什么信息都拿不到。更糟的是，它还会误导你。所以你可能有一个程序

cues.en: And the program says, oh, I'm spending all my time in this stuff, whereas secretly, you're actually spending your time in native code that's not even going to show up in a report. So this is really bad. This seems like a huge problem. We kind of turned lemons into lemonade here. And so here is what we do. Every single time we get a signal, we record the current time. That is, what is the time on the wall? And when we come back and we get a signal again, we compare.
cues.zh: 程序会说，哦，我所有时间都花在这上面，而实际上你偷偷地把时间花在了原生代码上，它甚至不会出现在报告里。这真的很糟糕。这看起来是个大问题。我们算是把柠檬变成了柠檬水。所以这就是我们的做法。每次收到信号时，我们记录当前时间。也就是，墙上的时间是多少？当我们回来再次收到信号时，我们比较

cues.en: and see how much time has elapsed. Now, if we're not interrupted, then it would be whatever the delay was, the actual interval of 0.1 seconds, for example. However, there could be a delay. And if there is a delay, we know that that delay is basically because it was executing native code. So then we can account for it. So we keep these separate counters.
cues.zh: 看看过去了多少时间。现在，如果我们没有被中断，那就会是原本的延迟，比如实际的 0.1 秒间隔。然而，可能会有延迟。如果有延迟，我们就知道那个延迟基本上是因为它在执行原生代码。于是我们就可以把它算进去。所以我们保持这些分开的计数器。

cues.en: We have a Python time counter and a C time counter. The Python time counter, we only increment by the actual sampling interval and we attribute the rest of the delay to the C time. Likewise, we can actually leverage the fact that we can measure this thing called virtual time, which is the amount of time that we have in fact spent running on the CPU and discover how much time the process spent in system time, that is to say doing IO or sleeping for some other reason.

cues.en: Right. That's a great question. So first, both CAUSE and Scalene are built on sampling. So sampling really means that you have very little impact from the profiler itself. That is to say, it didn't have an effect one way or the other on the reported results. With Scalene,
cues.zh: 对，这是个好问题。首先，CAUSE 和 Scalene 都基于采样。采样的意思是，性能分析器本身的影响非常小。分析器只是周期性地唤醒，做点事情。用 CAUSE 时，我们非常小心，确保它做的任何事情都没有偏差。也就是说，它不会以任何方式影响报告结果。至于 Scalene，

cues.en: we couldn't play the same tricks because you're doing stuff at a Python level. But again, it's sampling based, so it should wash out. cues.zh: 可视化这个很难。已经有很多信息要显示了。我们选择的做法就是，不报告置信度低的内容，因为那可能只是你本来就会遇到的波动。我认为这可能是合理的推进方式：让性能分析器在结果很可能是噪声时，拒绝把它们报告为可操作项。说得通。

cues.en: So we have a couple of questions that I think tie together two things that might actually also give you an opportunity to talk about some of your other research, which is, you mentioned the finding of Mitch and Mitch at all, that really small differences can kind of swamp the effects of even O3. And you're using tools like scaling and cause to make performance improvements to code, or to make changes to code that you hope will lead to performance improvements.
cues.zh: 所以我们有一些问题，我觉得它们把两件事联系起来，这可能也给你机会谈谈你其他的研究，也就是你提到Mitch和Mitch等人的发现，即非常小的差异可能会淹没甚至O3的效果。而你正在使用像scaling和cause这样的工具来提升代码性能，或者对代码做改动，希望带来性能提升。

cues.en: how do you know that you're not just hitting the same kinds of weird hardware effects when you, for example, change the number of threads? Yeah, that's a great question. So cause, in particular, actually turns out to, by design, have an effect where it's sort of immune to this problem. So the reason is that if you have a multi-threaded program,
cues.zh: 比如，当你改变线程数时，你怎么知道你不是只是遇到了同样的奇怪硬件效应？是的，这是个好问题。特别是cause，实际上设计上就有一种效果，使它某种程度上不受这个问题影响。原因是，如果你有一个多线程程序，

cues.en: and you're randomly interrupting it. So you're randomly picking things that are happening and you're randomly doing different sizes and different everything. Everything is unbiased and you're in effect getting different executions every time because of the concurrency. So intuitively, you're mixing things up constantly. So whatever code is running on the processor, whatever memory is currently being accessed, those things are changing all the time.
cues.zh: 并且你随机中断它。所以你随机挑选正在发生的事情，随机做不同的大小和不同的所有东西。一切都是无偏的，由于并发，你实际上每次都会得到不同的执行。所以直观地说，你在不断地打乱东西。所以无论处理器上运行什么代码，当前访问什么内存，这些东西都在不断变化。

cues.en: So that actually has the effect of giving you kind of a random, which I call it, it's sort of like an electron cloud in a sense of the distribution of everything. And so when you get points over time, it kind of factors out all of those effects. So it's a great question and it's spot on. So we had a paper where we also built the system and I didn't talk about it today for lack of time, but the results that we have for dash O two and dash O three,
cues.zh: 所以这实际上有一种效果，给你一种随机的，我称之为，在某种意义上像电子云一样的所有东西的分布。所以当你随时间得到点时，它有点把所有这些效应都分解掉了。所以这是个好问题，而且很准确。我们有一篇论文，我们也构建了系统，今天因为时间不够我没讲，但我们针对dash O2和dash O3得到的结果，

cues.en: I mentioned, you might not have noticed, that I factored out the effective memory layout. So we built this tool called Stabilizer, which does this by actually randomizing everything at runtime. So in a weird way, Stabilizer does it precisely. It does it for sequential program. It has a random placement of functions, random placement of the heap, random placement of globals, random placement of stack, and it does it over and over again.
cues.zh: 我提到过，你可能没注意到，我把有效内存布局分解掉了。所以我们构建了这个叫Stabilizer的工具，它通过在运行时随机化一切来做到这一点。所以奇怪的是，Stabilizer做得非常精确。它针对顺序程序做这个。它随机放置函数、随机放置堆、随机放置全局变量、随机放置栈，并且反复这样做。

cues.en: What happens with cause is that you get the benefit of that just by virtue of the fact that you're running concurrent code. So the concurrent code is causing this disruption, whereas stabilizer is going to work for sequential program as well. Hope that answers the question. Thanks. That's a great answer. The concern is a real one and I think you've given a good reason why we might be able to accommodate it.
cues.zh: CAUSE 的好处在于，你只要运行并发代码就能获得这种收益。所以是并发代码造成了这种干扰，而 stabilizer 对顺序程序也同样有效。希望这回答了你的问题。谢谢。这是个很好的回答。这种担忧是真实存在的，而且我认为你给出了一个很好的理由，说明我们为什么或许能够兼顾它。

cues.en: There's a few questions that are kind of related to something that I thought was interesting. It's something I hadn't even thought about until these questions came in about the interaction between cause and existing compiler optimizations. Are there kind of weird interactions that happen? Like if you turn on compiler optimizations will cause either give you an incorrect diagnosis of where an issue might be coming from.
cues.zh: 有几个问题跟我认为有趣的一件事相关。直到这些问题出现之前，我甚至都没想过这件事，就是 CAUSE 与现有编译器优化之间的相互作用。会不会出现奇怪的相互作用？比如，如果你开启编译器优化，CAUSE 会不会给出关于问题来源的错误诊断。

cues.en: Or does it affect what looks like the important parts of code? And then somebody asked a slightly different question, which is, could you use something like CAUSE to help target compiler optimization? So let's see. So CAUSE is really about identifying, you've got a program and you want to know what parts of it you should speed up, right? If you are going to apply CAUSE, you should definitely apply CAUSE with the optimized code that you'd be running in production. It doesn't make sense.
cues.zh: 或者它是否会影响代码中看起来重要的部分？然后有人问了一个稍微不同的问题，就是能否用类似 CAUSE 的东西来帮助定位编译器优化。我们来看看。CAUSE 的真正目的是识别——你有一个程序，你想知道应该加速它的哪些部分，对吧？如果你要应用 CAUSE，你绝对应该在实际生产环境中运行的优化后代码上应用 CAUSE。否则没有意义。

cues.en: to run cause with unoptimized code. In a sense, it's like you're performing an experiment on a pig, and you really want to see if the experiment applies to trees. It's just like, don't do that. You really want to run the experiment on the thing that you actually care about. So with respect to compiler optimizations,
cues.zh: 要在未优化的代码上运行cause。某种意义上，这就像你在一头猪身上做实验，却真的很想看看这个实验是否适用于树木。这就好比，别这么做。你真正想在你在意的东西上做实验。所以关于编译器优化，

cues.en: There's the layout stuff and compilers actually do take into account layout and try to do layout optimizations with mixed effects. Like I mentioned, these things are super brittle. Just the mere fact that you come in and your username is Homer and somebody else's username is Arun, it differs by one character. That one character is going to shift the stack and it can have a gigantic impact.
cues.zh: 还有布局方面的东西，编译器实际上会考虑布局，并尝试进行布局优化，但效果参差不齐。就像我提到的，这些东西非常脆弱。仅仅是你进来，你的用户名是Homer，别人的用户名是Arun，只差一个字符。那一个字符会移动栈的位置，可能产生巨大的影响。

cues.en: So I feel like that the effort that's spent on layout optimizations, people should be careful because unless you're running the same code all the time with very similar kind of size data, you'll get very different effects. So yeah, so I'm not sure that causes anything to say in particular about where compiler optimizers should work unless it's one of those situations like, boy, if I spend an hour in the compiler, like imagine, imagine the compiler could just go to town for an hour or a day.
cues.zh: 所以我觉得，人们在布局优化上投入的精力要小心，因为除非你一直运行相同的代码、数据规模也非常相似，否则你会得到截然不同的效果。所以，我不确定这能让cause特别说明编译器优化器应该在哪里工作，除非是那种情况，比如，天哪，如果我在编译器上花一个小时，想象一下，想象编译器可以尽情运行一个小时或一天。

cues.en: optimizing some code, and they just don't do it because nobody wants their compiler to be so slow. If you were willing to say, look, this code really matters to me. I'll be gone this weekend. You go optimize as much as you can, and I'll come back. That actually would be fine. I think many people would be happy with an optimizer where you could be like, I know you normally are trying to be nice and friendly to me, but you go crazy and spend a day, two days, a week running. That would be interesting.
cues.zh: 优化一些代码，而他们就是不这么做，因为没人希望自己的编译器那么慢。如果你愿意说，看，这段代码对我真的很重要。我这个周末不在。你尽可能多地优化，我回来。那其实没问题。我想很多人会乐于接受这样的优化器：你可以说，我知道你平时都尽量对我友好客气，但你就放开手脚，花一天、两天、一周去跑。那会很有意思。

cues.en: Thanks. I think we have time for one last quick question, and I'm choosing this one because I think it'll give you an opportunity to talk about yet another one of your cool pieces of work that's related. Somebody heard your discussion of stabilizer and asked, does the randomized placement of things you've mentioned have any implications for security? Right. Yes. Actually, when we wrote stabilizer, we were trying to decide whether we should pitch it as
cues.zh: 谢谢。我想我们还有时间再问最后一个简短问题，我选这个是因为我觉得它能让你有机会谈谈你另一项相关的很酷的工作。有人听了你对 Stabilizer 的讨论后问：你提到的这些对象的随机化放置，对安全有什么影响吗？对，是的。其实我们写 Stabilizer 时，正在纠结该把它宣传成

cues.en: the performance thing, which is what it was intended for, or a security thing, or both. And we decided that for cleanliness of discussion, we would just focus on the one thing. So we kept it as performance. But actually, re-randomization and so on, I mean, the amount of randomization Stabilizer produces is really, really high. And it's one of the first, it's definitely the first system out there to randomize things at runtime.
cues.zh: 性能工具——这本来就是它的目标——还是安全工具，或者两者兼顾。为了讨论清晰，我们决定只聚焦一点，所以保留了性能这个定位。但实际上，重新随机化之类的东西，我是说 Stabilizer 产生的随机化程度真的非常高。而且它是最早的系统之一，也绝对是第一个在运行时对对象进行随机化的系统。

cues.en: and so many of these things at runtime. So there's a whole line of these things that are called moving target defenses. So moving target defenses are exactly intended to thwart certain kinds of attacks. The Die Harder paper that Millen mentioned in the beginning is about a randomizing memory allocator specifically designed for security. So we have random allocation of things in space. There's guard pages. You can't predict.
cues.zh: 以及在运行时做这么多这类随机化。于是就有了整条被称为移动目标防御的路线。移动目标防御正是为了挫败某些类型的攻击。Millen 开头提到的 Die Harder 论文，讲的是一个专为安全设计的随机化内存分配器。所以我们会在空间上随机分配对象。还有保护页。你无法预测。

cues.en: Any more than you can predict a random number generator, its output, you can't predict what addresses things will be at. And so the likelihood of an attacker being able to safely exploit something where they have addresses or known offsets basically goes to zero. So yes, it definitely, lots of security implications for randomization. Thanks for that answer, Emory. And thanks for all of your answers and for talking about your amazing work and a lot of the other pieces of work that you've done. But I'm afraid we've run out of time.
cues.zh: 你无法像预测随机数生成器的输出那样预测对象的地址。因此，攻击者要想利用已知地址或偏移量来安全地实施攻击，其可能性基本为零。所以，随机化对安全性确实有着诸多影响。感谢你的解答，Emory。也感谢你所有的回答，以及分享你出色的工作和所做的许多其他工作。但恐怕我们的时间到了。
